Lessons.Title: Create Your Own Number Line
ExplanationParagraphs: First Edition 2021, Grade 3 Unit 8 Lesson 2. Learning goals: show fractions on a uniformly spaced number line and record comparisons using <, = and >. Source teacher lesson and preparation HTML inspected locally, with embedded pupil activity directions. The original student task PDF and four illustrated warm-up images were not visually audited; access them through the source with the teacher, not through fabricated visuals.

Warm-up (10 minutes): four original fraction-on-number-line pictures A-D invite more than one justified odd-one-out response. Students compare partition size, tick marks, whole-number anchors, labels and fraction locations. A specific A-D choice cannot be auto-graded without inspecting the four original image geometries.

Activity 1 (25 minutes): in groups of 3-4, build a LONG FLOOR number line with masking/painter tape and markers. Use consistent unit lengths and start with whole-number and unit-fraction benchmarks. Place all thirteen source fractions: 1/2, 1/3, 6/2, 12/3, 1/4, 5/4, 6/6, 5/6, 9/8, 15/8, 5/3, 18/6, 2/8. Label equivalent fractions at the same position (1/4 = 2/8 and 6/2 = 18/6). The source includes 12/3 = 4, so a line from 0 to 2 would be too short. Preserve all source quantities without replacing the physical construction by a single-answer screen question.

Number line verification: there are thirteen given representations but eleven distinct points. Points beyond 1 include 9/8, 5/4, 5/3, 15/8, and points at 3 and 4. Students can compare denominators of equal wholes, convert 6/2 = 3 and 12/3 = 4, and use consistent unit partitioning. Teacher assesses spacing, annotations, explanation and team contributions.

Activity 2 (10 minutes): using the very same group number line, pupils invent SIX comparison statements: two >, two =, two <; choose any TWO to justify through numbers, drawings or words. Answers depend on their self-generated pair choices; numerical-only automatic grading does not verify original creative work.

Independent Edulytics examples (not the original assigned response set): 6/2 = 18/6, 1/4 = 2/8, 12/3 > 6/2, 15/8 > 5/3, 1/3 < 1/2, 5/6 < 6/6. For each show why positions on a shared calibrated number line establish the relationship; other valid statements remain possible.

Synthesis (teacher facilitated): students discuss why the floor line must accommodate its greatest number, and why changing the physical line length with consistently equal unit intervals does not change fraction ordering. Compare strategies rather than imposing a single response.

The original publisher Cool-down Where Do I Go? is access-gated and not included here. Use a separate first-party self-check after the lesson; teacher review remains required for original diagram, tape construction, explanations and comparisons. No publisher images or teacher-only Cool-down are copied. Runtime tests, teacher approval and Stage D remain separate.

KeyConcepts.Title: Consistent whole-unit scaling
KeyConcepts.Definition: All consecutive whole-number marks are separated by an equal distance.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Include 0 through 4 so every source value can be placed.
KeyConcepts.Example: 12/3 = 4 must fit on the same line as 1/4 and 15/8.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equivalent positions
KeyConcepts.Definition: Equivalent fractions have the same point on the number line.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Do not place equal fractions at different coordinates.

KeyConcepts.Title: Comparisons
KeyConcepts.Definition: Comparison symbols describe the relative ordered positions of two numbers.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Provide exactly two true statements for each of >, = and <, then justify two.

WorkedExamples.Title: Place the source fractions
WorkedExamples.Question: Where do 6/2, 18/6, 12/3, 1/4, and 2/8 belong?
WorkedExamples.Method: Simplify rational values, then place equal values at shared coordinates.
Steps: Build a line of equal whole-number intervals 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
Locate 1/4 and 2/8 at the same quarter point.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Both fractions at 3, one fraction at 4, both quarter fractions at 1/4.
WorkedExamples.Check: A 0-to-2-only line would omit the original 12/3 and 6/2.

WorkedExamples.Title: Create and defend two comparisons
WorkedExamples.Question: Give examples of two equality, two greater-than and two less-than statements.
WorkedExamples.Method: Check each relationship using the same whole unit and equivalent fractions.
Steps: Compare 6/2 with 18/6, then 1/4 with 2/8 for two equalities.
Compare 12/3 with 6/2, then 15/8 with 5/3 for two > statements.
Compare 1/3 with 1/2, then 5/6 with 6/6 for two < statements.
Explain why at least two of the six comparisons hold using partitioned intervals.
WorkedExamples.Check: These are invented first-party examples, not the only original student answers.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Draw a line only from 0 to 2.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Find the maximum source value first, and extend the whole-number intervals through 4.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Two pairs of source fractions are equivalent.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Overlay 2/8 with 1/4 and 18/6 with 6/2; there are 11 locations.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Use different distances for the same whole-unit interval.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The lengths would no longer represent consistent numerical differences.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Grade a self-invented comparison by one predefined answer.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Any correctly reasoned six statements with the required two-per-symbol counts qualify.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use a teacher checklist for mathematically true statements and two explanations.

SummaryPoints: Warm-up four source images need teacher verification; open odd-one-out reasons.
Construct and label all 13 original source fractions on one physical number line.
Generate 6 true comparisons: 2 each of <, = and >; explain 2.
Source materials from local 2021 teacher HTML. Original student PDF and figure pixels are unverified; gated source Cool-down omitted.
